blueprint_topic: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — ketamine respiratory safety and monitoring
stem: A client is receiving ketamine hydrochloride for a procedure. The nurse notes that pharyngeal and laryngeal reflexes may remain active with this medication. Which interpretation is most accurate?

options.A: Preserved upper-airway reflexes make respiratory monitoring unnecessary during ketamine administration because clinically important respiratory depression cannot occur while reflexes remain active.
options.B: Ketamine may preserve pharyngeal and laryngeal reflexes but can still cause respiratory depression; continuously monitor the client and keep emergency airway equipment immediately available.
options.C: Preserved pharyngeal and laryngeal reflexes make ketamine appropriate as the sole anesthetic for procedures involving mechanical stimulation of the pharynx, larynx, or bronchial tree.
options.D: Respiratory support is needed only after protective airway reflexes disappear completely, so oxygenation and ventilation do not require attention while those reflexes remain present.

rationale: Current ketamine hydrochloride injection labeling states that pharyngeal and laryngeal reflexes are not suppressed when ketamine is used alone, but respiratory depression may occur, particularly with overdosage or an overly rapid administration rate. The label requires continuous vital-sign monitoring and immediate availability of emergency airway equipment, and it advises avoiding ketamine as the sole anesthetic for procedures involving the pharynx, larynx, or bronchial tree. Therefore B is correct. A and D wrongly equate preserved reflexes with absence of respiratory risk, and C directly conflicts with the procedural warning.
educational_objective: Recognize that ketamine may preserve pharyngeal and laryngeal reflexes yet still requires continuous monitoring and immediate airway readiness because respiratory depression can occur.
source_organization: DailyMed (U.S. National Library of Medicine) / FDA labeling
source_document_title: KETAMINE HYDROCHLORIDE injection — Full Prescribing Information
source_version_date: Current prescribing information dated April 9, 2026; accessed 2026-08-26
source_locator: Dosage and Administration §2.1 — continuously monitor vital signs; emergency airway equipment immediately available. Warnings and Precautions §5.3 — respiratory depression may occur with overdosage or rapid administration; maintain oxygenation/ventilation. §5.4 — pharyngeal/laryngeal reflexes are not suppressed; avoid sole use for procedures of pharynx, larynx, or bronchial tree.
source_claim_supported: Ketamine may preserve pharyngeal and laryngeal reflexes but can still cause respiratory depression; continuous monitoring and immediate airway support capability are required, and ketamine alone should be avoided for procedures involving the pharynx/larynx/bronchial tree.
blueprint_locator: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies, printed p.12/PDF p.16: administer high-risk medications safely; monitor adverse effects and evaluate client response.
candidate_reasons_resolved: Rewrote all four choices as substantive respiratory-safety interpretations without absolute-word distractor cues.
Balanced option length and used a current April 2026 label while preserving the distinction between airway-reflex preservation and respiratory safety.
audit_note: Independent adversarial review confirms B uniquely reflects current ketamine labeling. All options are tightly length-matched, and preserved reflexes are not misrepresented as protection from respiratory depression.
